newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: By Lien van der Leij.
newsitem.headline: By Lien van der Leij.

text.p: Amsterdam Exchanges on Thursday unveiled its latest initiative in the battle for European market share in Dutch securities with the launch of a new market for young, fast-growing companies hungry for capital.

Dubbed New Market Amsterdam or NMAX, the market is geared to young Dutch companies which are currently forced to look for capital on foreign markets such as NASDAQ or London's Alternative Investment Market (AIM), the bourse's general director Hans Brouwer told a news conference.
"Companies are crossing the Atlantic to seek a listing on NASDAQ...(because) the threshold for going public in the Netherlands is currently relatively high," Brouwer said.

The entry criteria for NMAX, set to list its first company in early March, are less stringent than for the Official Market, reflecting the listed companies' relatively higher level of risk -- and potential return.
To gain a listing on NMAX, companies must have existed for three years -- but need not have shown a profit.
"Like NASDAQ, NMAX focuses on a company's future potential, rather than its track record," Brouwer said.

The shareholders' equity requirement for listed companies is also significantly lower than for the Official Market at just two million guilders versus ten million. However, two million guilders' worth of the equity must also be freely tradeable.
Investors are offered some safeguards in the form of a quarterly reporting requirement and a capital "lock-up".

Under the lock-up requirement, corporate shareholders at the time of listing owning more than a five percent interest must commit themselves not to dispose of their holdings until the firm is profitable.
After the first profitable year they may cash in no more than 50 percent of their holding, and may dispose of the rest after three years in profit.
In addition, the bank or broker managing the initial public offering must commit to guiding its debutant for the first three years and to making a market in the stock.
The new market forms part of a larger European initiative with Paris, Frankfurt and Brussels called Euro.NM.
So far only Paris' Nouveau Marche is up and running, but the ultimate objective is an interconnected European platform of exchanges with dealers in each able to trade on all four.
The Nouveau Marche was launched on February 14 last year, and was developing according to plan, Nouveau Marche director Dominic Leblanc said.
So far 19 companies -- 17 of them French -- have acquired an NM listing representing total market capitalisation of 1.6 billion French francs.
A further 30 to 40 companies are in line for a listing over the next year.
Germany's equivalent Neuer Markt is set to launch on March 10 with two companies listed, while a further 10-20 companies are expected to join during the first year.
In Belgium the first New Market listing is expected "during the course of March" with a further five companies set to follow soon afterwards.
The first NMAX listing in the Netherlands will be Polydoc, a Dutch-based software house already quoted on London's AIM.
"We launched on AIM last year because we had no recourse to the Dutch capital market at that time," said Polydoc's chief executive officer Richard Madox.

Polydoc, set up three years ago with funds from the European Eureka development programme, numbers Dutch chemicals firm DSM and civil service pension fund ABP amongst its clients and therefore wished to develop a Dutch capital base, Madox said.
Second in line for a NMAX listing is agri hi-tech firm Proline, whose products include fully-computerised milking machines. It is set to list early in April.
Amsterdam Stock Exchanges' Brouwer said there were dozens of young, fast-growing Dutch firms eligible for NMAX listing.
"It's up to us -- the banks, intermediaries and the exchanges -- to seek them out," he said. "We're not sitting back and waiting for them to come to us."
